name: Aram
title: Son of Shem and ancestor of the Arameans
lifespan: Unknown; biblical chronology places him in the generations shortly after the Flood
summary: Aram belonged to the second generation after Noah and was one of five sons born to Shem. Through his four sons—Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash—he was regarded as the ancestor of the Aramean peoples who settled in Syria and northern Mesopotamia. The geographical region of Aram was named after him, and his descendants developed the Aramaic language, which over time became the most important common language in the Middle East. In the biblical narrative, the Aramean connection is of great significance: Israel's own patriarchs had close family ties to the Aramean region, and the Arameans appear repeatedly as both allies and opponents throughout the history of the Old Testament.
roles: Part of the genealogy following Noah

keyEvents.title: Aram's Place in the Genealogy
keyEvents.description: Aram is mentioned as one of Shem's five sons in the genealogy after the flood, where the nations of the world are traced back to Noah's three sons.

keyEvents.title: Aram's Four Sons
keyEvents.description: Aram's sons—Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash—are regarded as ancestors of various ethnic groups in the Aramean region, and their names are linked to geographical regions in Syria and Mesopotamia.

keyEvents.title: Confirmation in the Genealogies of Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Aram's lineage is repeated in the genealogies of Chronicles, where his place among Shem's sons and his descendants are confirmed.

keyEvents.title: The Aramean Geographical Legacy
keyEvents.description: The region of Aram-Naharaim, bearing Aram's name, plays an important role in the patriarchal narratives. It was to this area that Abraham's servant was sent to find a wife for Isaac, showing the enduring connection between Israel's ancestors and the Aramean heartland.

versions.summary: Aram was one of Shem's five sons and a grandson of Noah. He is regarded as the ancestor of the Aramean peoples and the Aramaic-speaking region in Mesopotamia and Syria. His descendants played a significant role in biblical history, especially through the Arameans as neighbors to Israel.
versions.title: Son of Shem and ancestor of the Arameans
versions.reason: [major] Genesis 11:10-11 deals generally with Shem's age and sons (Arpachshad), but does not specifically mention Aram. Aram is not mentioned in the detailed genealogy of Genesis 11, which follows the line Shem → Arpachshad → Shelah → Eber etc. This event is incorrect and should be removed or corrected.; [major] The Aram mentioned in Luke 3:33 (and Matthew 1:3-4) is a completely different person – Ram/Aram from the tribe of Judah, son of Hezron. Including this as a key event for Shem's son Aram is misleading and should be removed, as it creates confusion between two different biblical figures.; [minor] In addition to 'patriarch', the role 'ancestor' can be added to clarify his function as the forefather of the Arameans, which is distinct from the patriarch role in the narrow sense.; [minor] The summary is good, but could specify that the Aramaic language became a lingua franca over large parts of the Middle East and was also used in parts of the Old Testament (Ezra, Daniel).; [minor] Lifespan is speculative since the Bible does not give Aram's age. The dating is based on chronological estimates and should be regarded as very approximate.; [minor] The children's names 'Uz', 'Hul', 'Gether' and 'Mash' are acceptable Norwegian forms. In some translations 'Mas' is used instead of 'Mash', and in 1 Chronicles 1:17 'Mash' is called 'Meshech'. This may be worth noting.

footnotes.text: The name 'Aram' is linked to the geographical region of Aram, which in biblical times covered much of present-day Syria and northern Mesopotamia. In Akkadian, the area is known as 'Aramu', and it is mentioned in Assyrian source texts from the 12th century BCE onward.

The Aramaic language, traditionally linked to Aram's descendants, became the dominant lingua franca in the Middle East from around the 700s BCE. Parts of the Old Testament (including Ezra 4:8–6:18, 7:12–26; Daniel 2:4–7:28) are written in Aramaic, and it was likely Jesus' everyday language.

In 1 Chronicles 1:17, 'Mash' is listed among Aram's sons instead of 'Meshech' as in Genesis 10:23. This may be due to a textual variant, and scholars discuss whether this refers to the same person under different name forms.

The Arameans appear as a significant people in biblical history, notably through the kingdom of Aram-Damascus, which was an important regional power and frequent rival to Israel and Judah during the monarchy (cf. 2 Sam 8; 1 Kings 20; 2 Kings 5–8).

According to Deuteronomy 26:5, the Israelites were to confess: "My father was a wandering Aramean." This links Israel's patriarchs to the Aramean region, as both Rebekah, Leah, and Rachel had an Aramean background through Laban.

Archaeological findings from the Tel Dan Stele (c. 840 BC), erected by an Aramean king (likely Hazael of Damascus), confirm the political power of the Arameans and their interaction with Israelite kingdoms.

The rabbinic tradition counts Aram among the 70 nations descended from Noah's sons after the flood. The genealogy in Genesis 10 (often called the 'Table of Nations') has been the subject of extensive rabbinic commentary, linking each patriarch to specific peoples and territories.
